newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea arrests three union leaders, offers talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea arrests three union leaders, offers talks.

text.p: Police arrested three South Korean union leaders for leading strikes at a shipyard but the chairman of the ruling New Korea Party said on Thursday he still wanted dialogue to avert a crisis over a controversial labour law.

One day after state prosecutors issued an ultimatum to strike leaders to drop industrial action immediately or face arrest, Lee Hong-koo promised steps to allay worker fears the legislation could lead to layoffs.
"I would like to use this occasion to make it known again my willingness to resolve all problems through dialogue and compromise," Lee told a news conference.

Ealier, prosecution officials said police arrested three union leaders of Halla Heavy Industries overnight on charges of obstructing business. This brings to four the number of union heads seized in the past 48 hours.
The three were also accused of beating up workers who refused to down tools at the shipyard in the southwestern town of Yongam, one official said.
Another Halla Heavy union leader was arrested on Tuesday night on similar charges, the official said.

But seven leaders of an outlawed umbrella union group, spearheading three weeks of strikes demanding the repeal of the new law, continued to take sanctuary on the icy grounds of Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral.
In all, 16 union leaders are still being sought by state prosecutors for organising wildcat strikes that began immediately after the labour bill was passed.
Lee repeated his offer of a televised debate with union leaders for "a right judgement by the people" and called on the opposition to begin dialogue.

Lee said he regretted opposition parties did not agree to pass the new law, which allows companies to lay off workers and replace striking workers, while banning multiple union representation for three years.
"As the chairman of the ruling party that spearheaded the labour legislation I offer to the people words of humble regret," he said.
The bill was rammed through parliament at a six-minute dawn session in the absence of opposition deputies on December 26.
"If there are disadvantages caused by this labour legislation, I and the New Korea Party will lead efforts to minimise them," he said.
"We will do our utmost to prepare various follow-up steps to end fears of employment and the problem of unemployment."
However, Lee ruled out revising the law, saying he was convinced it was "an inevitable choice for an economic recovery and a new leap forward".
"Therefore I would like to make it clear that our party has no intention to revise the labour law at this point," he said.
Seven shaven-headed leaders of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions on Thursday reaffirmed that its members would start all-out strikes if they were arrested.
The confederation backed down from its earlier threats of a general strike, including a public-sector shutdown, on Wednesday when its calls for all-out stoppages went largely unheeded.
Hospital workers on Thursday reported to work and the country's largest union group, the government-sanctioned Federation of Korean Trade Unions, ended a two-day stoppage.
On Wednesday, cabinet ministers said the government would crack down on illegal strikes which they said undermined the already slowing economy.
